chunks: "Subharmonic oscillation is an instability of fixed-frequency peak current-mode control where the inductor current and duty cycle alternate cycle by cycle, so you get a pattern of a long pulse, a short pulse, a long pulse, repeating at half the switching frequency.
Here's why. In peak current mode the high side turns on at each clock edge and turns off when the inductor current hits the control level.
Suppose in one cycle the starting current is a little higher than normal by delta.
It reaches the threshold sooner, by delta over m1 where m1 is the rising slope, so the on-time is shorter, and the off-time is longer by that same amount.
During the longer off-time the current falls at m2, the falling slope, so it falls an extra m2 times delta over m1.
So at the start of the next cycle the error is minus m2 over m1 times delta: the sign flips, and the size is multiplied by m2 over m1.
With the slopes in terms of duty cycle, m2 over m1 is D over one minus D.
If D is below 50 percent, that factor is less than one, so the error shrinks every cycle and the converter is stable.

At exactly 50 percent it neither grows nor shrinks, and above 50 percent it grows, so the pulses alternate wider and narrower with growing amplitude until something nonlinear limits it, like a skipped pulse or the clamp.
The fix is slope compensation: add an artificial ramp to the sensed current, or subtract it from the command, so the threshold falls during the on-time.
That changes the factor to minus m2 minus m a over m1 plus m a, which can be made less than one for any duty cycle."
